name: Benzphetamine

lead: Benzphetamine (Didrex) is an older prescription appetite suppressant related to amphetamine. It reduces hunger so people eat less and lose weight, working toward a leaner look.

It is thought to increase norepinephrine and dopamine release in the brain's feeding centers, and the body converts it to amphetamine and methamphetamine. In the US it is labelled as a short-term add-on, lasting a few weeks, to a reduced-calorie diet for people with a BMI of 30 or higher.

paras: It is taken as a pill under prescription for a short period alongside a calorie-restricted diet. The label states it is not for long-term use.

Reported effects include raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia and restlessness. The label cites an association between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension and contraindicates use in pregnancy. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US.

angle.text: Benzphetamine is a stimulant appetite suppressant that lowers calorie intake and leads to weight loss and a leaner look. It is a prescription obesity medication labelled for a few weeks of use.

lead: Benzphetamine (brand name Didrex, also spelled benzfetamine) is a prescription appetite suppressant. It is used to reduce hunger so that a person eating fewer calories can lose body fat, which in turn changes how the face and body look: a smaller waist, a slimmer face and more visible muscle definition. In the United States it is labelled as a short-term adjunct, a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted weight-reduction regimen for adults with a body mass index of 30 or higher who have not responded to diet and exercise alone.[1][2]

It belongs to the sympathomimetic amine class alongside phentermine, diethylpropion and phendimetrazine, the older anorectics approved only for short-term use.[3][4] It is described as a prodrug that the body converts into amphetamine and methamphetamine, and it is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US, which Wikipedia notes is unusual for an amphetamine-related drug.[2][2]

Benzphetamine is a medical drug, not a cosmetic product, and the label does not describe it for cosmetic weight reduction.[1][2] Within appearance and bodybuilding culture it appears mostly as one of the older fat-loss prescription stimulants, and it is also named on anti-doping prohibited-stimulant lists that circulate in training forums.[5]
infobox: Schedule III controlled substance, prescription only

paras: The US label indicates benzphetamine for the management of exogenous obesity as a short-term adjunct to caloric restriction in patients with a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to appropriate weight-reduction efforts.[1] Reviews group it with diethylpropion, phendimetrazine and phentermine as the sympathomimetic drugs approved only for short-term use, in contrast with newer medications approved for longer treatment.[3][4]

Grokipedia reports that the drug was approved in 1960 and that trials showed modest additional weight loss over placebo that plateaued after the early weeks as tolerance developed; that source is AI-generated and these figures were not checked against trial reports.[6]

The label states that in short-term trials people taking the drug lost more weight than people on placebo plus the same diet, but that the difference amounted to a fraction of a pound per week; weight loss was greatest in the first weeks and varied between trials. It adds that obesity is a long-term condition while the trials lasted only weeks, so the benefit over diet alone is described as limited.[1] The label also says treatment should continue only if the patient loses at least 4 pounds in the first 4 weeks, and that if the appetite-suppressing effect fades, the dose should not be raised to regain it; the drug is instead discontinued.[1]

Appetite suppressants are discussed as adjuncts to diet and physical activity, and a drug-insight review describes them as helpful adjuncts for selected patients aiming to achieve and maintain weight loss.[4] Any change in appearance from benzphetamine comes through that fat loss. The US label states the drug is intended for obesity management rather than cosmetic use.[1]
A 2025 editorial in Cureus discusses a theoretical case for benzphetamine in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, reasoning from its amphetamine-like pharmacology; it is not an approved use.[7]

The label lists palpitations, tachycardia and elevated blood pressure among cardiovascular effects, along with central nervous system effects such as overstimulation, restlessness and insomnia.[1] It warns against combining benzphetamine with other anorectic agents, including over-the-counter and herbal products.[1]

By body system, the label lists cardiovascular effects (palpitations, tachycardia, raised blood pressure, with isolated reports of cardiomyopathy and ischaemic events with chronic amphetamine use), central nervous system effects (overstimulation, restlessness, dizziness, insomnia, tremor, sweating, headache; rarely psychotic episodes, with depression possible after withdrawal), gastrointestinal effects (dry mouth, unpleasant taste, nausea, diarrhoea), allergic skin reactions such as hives, and changes in libido.[1]

Drug interactions listed on the label include monoamine oxidase inhibitors (hypertensive crises are described with concurrent use or within 14 days of an MAOI) and other stimulants. The label also notes that amphetamines can reduce the effect of some antihypertensive drugs, that insulin requirements may change as weight falls, and that urinary pH can alter drug levels.[1]

The label cites a case-control study in which anorectic drugs used for longer than three months were associated with a 23-fold increase in the risk of pulmonary hypertension, a rare and often fatal condition.[1] Valvular heart disease has been reported with some other anorectics such as fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine; the label states that no such cases had been reported with benzphetamine.[1] The drug is contraindicated in pregnancy.[1] Contraindications also include advanced arteriosclerosis, symptomatic cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, agitation, a history of drug misuse and recent monoamine oxidase inhibitor use.[2]

A review of obesity-drug safety notes that the safety record of obesity drugs has historically been poor, citing withdrawn drugs, and reviews the safety of benzphetamine among the currently available agents.[8] Wikipedia lists dependence liability as high.[2]

The label's section on abuse and dependence says that because benzphetamine is chemically and pharmacologically related to the amphetamines it carries abuse potential, that some patients have taken many times the recommended amount, and that stopping abruptly after prolonged high intake is followed by marked fatigue and low mood. Chronic intoxication with this class is described as causing insomnia, irritability, skin problems, personality change and, in its most severe form, psychosis resembling schizophrenia.[1]

Benzphetamine is a sympathomimetic amine. Wikipedia describes it as thought to stimulate release of norepinephrine and dopamine in the lateral hypothalamus, an effect attributed to binding the vesicular monoamine transporter VMAT2 and inhibiting its function, which reduces appetite.[2][2] The US label notes it stimulates the central nervous system and raises blood pressure, and adds that its weight-reducing action may not be due to appetite suppression alone, since other central or metabolic effects might contribute.[1] Tolerance and tachyphylaxis to the effect are described for the class.[1][2]

It is a prodrug: the body converts it to dextroamphetamine and dextromethamphetamine, which is why Wikipedia describes its dependence liability as high even though it is scheduled below amphetamine itself.[2] Wikipedia gives an elimination half-life of about 4 to 6 hours and plasma protein binding of 75 to 99 percent; the label states that human pharmacokinetic data are not available, and Grokipedia gives a longer half-life, so published figures differ.[1][2][6] A 1987 controlled human laboratory study examined the reinforcing and subjective effects of four anorectics, benzphetamine among them, in healthy volunteers.[9]

Benzphetamine is N-benzyl-N-methyl-1-phenylpropan-2-amine, the benzyl derivative of methamphetamine, with molecular formula C17H21N and a molar mass of about 239.4 g/mol; the form used clinically is the (S)-enantiomer, sold as the hydrochloride salt. Its International Nonproprietary Name is benzfetamine.[2][2] It is the parent compound of the related anorectic clobenzorex.[2]

Grokipedia gives a US approval year of 1960.[6] Legal status varies: Schedule III in the US, Schedule I in Canada, Class C in the UK, prescription-only (Schedule 4) in Australia, Class F2 in Brazil, and restricted to authorised scientific use in Germany.[2] It is the parent compound of the related anorectic clobenzorex.[2]

Benzphetamine appears on World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited stimulant lists that T Nation members have posted in supplement and drug-testing threads, and a 2003 thread lists Didrex among several prescription drugs a poster described holding.[5][10]

Benzphetamine is one of the older sympathomimetic anorectics, sold in the US under the brand Didrex among others. Reviews of obesity pharmacotherapy group it with phentermine, diethylpropion and phendimetrazine as the short-term drugs that predate the newer agents approved for longer-term treatment, and a safety review of obesity drugs notes that the field has a history of withdrawals for cardiovascular harm, such as the fenfluramine drugs that the label itself distinguishes from benzphetamine.[1][3][4][8]
The Medical Letter's periodic reviews of drugs and devices for weight management, published in 2022 and 2025, place the older sympathomimetics alongside newer incretin-based medicines.[11][12]

Benzphetamine is Schedule III in the United States, unusual among amphetamine-related drugs, most of which are Schedule II. It is Class C in the UK, Schedule I in Canada, Schedule 4 (prescription only) in Australia, Class F2 in Brazil and limited to authorised scientific use in Germany.[2]

Benzphetamine appears on World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited stimulant lists that members of T Nation reposted in threads about supplements, wrestling and drug testing between 2004 and 2011.[5][13][14] A 2003 thread listed Didrex among several prescription drugs a member said he held, and the question was how they might fit into bodybuilding.[10]

Published human work includes a 1969 controlled trial comparing single and divided doses of benzphetamine hydrochloride for pharmacodynamic activity, and a 1987 controlled trial of the reinforcing and subjective effects of benzphetamine, mazindol, phenylpropanolamine and phenmetrazine in healthy volunteers.[9][15] The US label summarises the older weight-loss trials qualitatively, reporting modest extra weight loss over placebo in the first weeks of treatment.[1] Reviews of weight-loss pharmacotherapy summarise it as one of the short-term sympathomimetic options.[3][4] A 2025 Cureus editorial discusses a theoretical potential in ADHD.[7] No studies found examining benzphetamine for facial appearance or cosmetic outcomes.

lore.intro: Benzphetamine is rarely the subject of looksmaxxing threads; in bodybuilding forums it turns up in lists of banned stimulants and in poster inventories of prescription drugs.[5][10]
